Amazon EKS AWS Load Balancer Controller ~25 minutes

ALB Ingress Runbook

Your app is running in the cluster but nobody outside can reach it. These seven steps put an Application Load Balancer in front of it and give you a public URL. Every command is meant to be copied as-is, and every step tells you how to check it worked before you move on.

Before you start

  • □An EKS cluster that is ACTIVE, with nodes in Ready state.
  • □kubectl get nodes works from your terminal.
  • □AWS CLI v2, configured and pointing at the right account.
  • □helm and eksctl installed.
  • □Your app already deployed — a Deployment and a Service. A plain ClusterIP Service is fine; the ALB does not need NodePort or LoadBalancer.
Read this first

Steps 1–5 are done once per cluster. Step 6 is done once per application. Nothing here is repeated on every deploy.

The order matters more than usual. Doing step 5 before step 2 gives you a controller that starts perfectly, reports no errors, and never creates a load balancer. Almost every failure in this process is silent — that is why each step ends with a check.

0

Set your variables

Everything below reuses these

Type these four values once. Every later command reads them, so a typo fails here — loudly and immediately — instead of halfway through step 4, where a mistyped cluster name produces an IAM role that looks correct and silently never works.

terminalbash
# Change these two to match your setup
export REGION=ap-south-1
export CLUSTER=my-cluster
export NAMESPACE=demo

# These two are derived - do not type them by hand
export ACCOUNT=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)
export VPC=$(aws eks describe-cluster --name "$CLUSTER" --region "$REGION" \
  --query "cluster.resourcesVpcConfig.vpcId" --output text)

echo "account=$ACCOUNT  cluster=$CLUSTER  vpc=$VPC  region=$REGION"
Check

The echo prints a real account id and a vpc-… id. If vpc= is empty, the cluster name is wrong — run aws eks list-clusters --region "$REGION" and use exactly what it prints.

Trap

These variables live in this terminal only. Close it, reboot, or open a second tab and they are gone — and the next command silently runs with an empty value. If you come back later, run this block again before anything else.

1

Register the cluster's OIDC provider

So pods can hold an AWS identity

The controller you are about to install is a pod, and it has to call AWS APIs to build a load balancer. It gets permission through IRSA — IAM Roles for Service Accounts — which needs your cluster registered in IAM as an identity provider.

Creating a cluster does not do this. The cluster has an OIDC issuer URL from day one, but IAM has never heard of it until you say so. This is the single most common reason "the controller starts but nothing happens".

terminalcheck first
# What the cluster says its issuer is
aws eks describe-cluster --name "$CLUSTER" --region "$REGION" \
  --query "cluster.identity.oidc.issuer" --output text

# Is that URL registered in IAM?
aws iam list-open-id-connect-providers

If the issuer is not in that list, register it:

terminalonly if missing
eksctl utils associate-iam-oidc-provider \
  --cluster "$CLUSTER" --region "$REGION" --approve
Check

Re-run list-open-id-connect-providers. One ARN must end with the same string the issuer URL ends with, minus the https://: 

issuer  https://oidc.eks.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/id/FDE3CE4E4283…
arn     arn:aws:iam::123456789012:oidc-provider/oidc.eks.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/id/FDE3CE4E4283…
Worth knowing

An account can hold several OIDC providers, each for a different issuer. If you also use GitHub Actions with OIDC, you will see token.actions.githubusercontent.com in that same list. Same mechanism, different issuer — one is for pods, one is for CI jobs.

2

Tag your subnets

The controller finds subnets by tag, not by asking you

You never tell the controller which subnets to put the load balancer in. It discovers them by reading AWS resource tags. No tags means it finds nothing, creates nothing, and reports nothing.

First: which subnets are really public?

A subnet is public if its route table has a route to an Internet Gateway. Not because it is named "public", and not because MapPublicIpOnLaunch is true — that flag only controls whether EC2 instances get an auto-assigned public IP, and an ALB brings its own. Ask AWS which is which:

terminaldiscover
# Subnets routed through an Internet Gateway = public
aws ec2 describe-route-tables --region "$REGION" \
  --filters "Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC" "Name=route.gateway-id,Values=igw-*" \
  --query "RouteTables[].Associations[].SubnetId" --output text

# Subnets routed through a NAT Gateway = private
aws ec2 describe-route-tables --region "$REGION" \
  --filters "Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC" "Name=route.nat-gateway-id,Values=nat-*" \
  --query "RouteTables[].Associations[].SubnetId" --output text

Then: tag them

terminalpaste your own subnet ids
export PUB1=subnet-aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa
export PUB2=subnet-bbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbb
export PVT1=subnet-ccccccccccccccccc
export PVT2=subnet-ddddddddddddddddd

# Public -> internet-facing load balancers
aws ec2 create-tags --region "$REGION" --resources $PUB1 $PUB2 \
  --tags Key=kubernetes.io/role/elb,Value=1

# Private -> internal load balancers. Not needed today, but tag it now
# so subnet roles are one lesson instead of two.
aws ec2 create-tags --region "$REGION" --resources $PVT1 $PVT2 \
  --tags Key=kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb,Value=1
Check 
aws ec2 describe-subnets --region "$REGION" \
  --subnet-ids $PUB1 $PUB2 $PVT1 $PVT2 \
  --query "Subnets[].{Subnet:SubnetId,AZ:AvailabilityZone,\
elb:Tags[?Key=='kubernetes.io/role/elb']|[0].Value,\
internal:Tags[?Key=='kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb']|[0].Value}" \
  --output table

You need two subnets with elb: 1, in two different Availability Zones. An ALB is a regional service and refuses to be created in a single AZ — one tagged subnet is not enough, no matter how correct it looks.

Trap

There is a third tag, kubernetes.io/cluster/<cluster-name>. You do not need it when one cluster owns the VPC — and if you add it with the wrong cluster name, that subnet is excluded from discovery. Leave it off unless you run two clusters in one VPC.

3

Create the IAM policy

What the controller is allowed to do

The controller calls EC2, ELB and ACM APIs on your behalf. AWS publishes the exact policy it needs — download it, do not hand-write it. Pin it to the same version as the chart you are about to install, so the policy and the code agree about which API calls exist.

terminalfind the version
helm repo add eks https://aws.github.io/eks-charts
helm repo update
helm search repo eks/aws-load-balancer-controller --versions | head -3

Read the APP VERSION column, then:

terminalcreate the policy
export LBC_VERSION=v3.5.0     # <- from the APP VERSION column

curl -sL -o alb-iam-policy.json \
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes-sigs/aws-load-balancer-controller/${LBC_VERSION}/docs/install/iam_policy.json"

head -3 alb-iam-policy.json

aws iam create-policy \
  --policy-name AWSLoadBalancerControllerIAMPolicy \
  --policy-document file://alb-iam-policy.json
Check

head -3 must print JSON starting with "Version": "2012-10-17". The command then prints the new policy's ARN — note it, step 4 needs it.

Trap

curl -sL is silent. A wrong version tag fetches GitHub's 404 web page and saves it as alb-iam-policy.json. create-policy then fails complaining about a malformed document and says nothing about the URL. That is what the head -3 is for.

Already exists from another cluster? That is fine — this policy is account-wide and shared. Skip the create and reuse the ARN.

4

Create the role and ServiceAccount

The IRSA link — one command, three objects

terminaleksctl
eksctl create iamserviceaccount \
  --cluster "$CLUSTER" \
  --region "$REGION" \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --name aws-load-balancer-controller \
  --attach-policy-arn "arn:aws:iam::${ACCOUNT}:policy/AWSLoadBalancerControllerIAMPolicy" \
  --override-existing-serviceaccounts \
  --approve

What that one command created

IAM role
eksctl-<cluster>-addon-iamserviceaccount-…
├─ trust policy — who may become this role
Condition
sub = system:serviceaccount:kube-system:aws-load-balancer-controller
├─ permission policy — what it may do
Attached
AWSLoadBalancerControllerIAMPolicy
└─ and in Kubernetes:
ServiceAccount
kube-system/aws-load-balancer-controller
annotation: eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn
The idea in one line

A role has two policies and beginners conflate them constantly. The trust policy answers who can become this role. The permission policy answers what the role can do. IRSA is entirely about the first one.

Nothing is stored anywhere. The pod presents a token signed by the cluster, AWS verifies the signature against the OIDC provider from step 1, checks the service account name against the trust policy, and hands back temporary credentials. No access key exists at any point.

Check 
kubectl get sa aws-load-balancer-controller -n kube-system \
  -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.eks\.amazonaws\.com/role-arn}{"\n"}'

This must print a role ARN. If it prints a blank line, stop here. The service account exists without its annotation, the controller will start and look healthy, and every single AWS call it makes will fail — which reads like a bug in the controller.

Trap

eksctl builds this as a CloudFormation stack, not a bare role. Running the command a second time errors instead of doing nothing, and deleting the cluster leaves the stack behind. To check or clean up, look for a stack named eksctl-$CLUSTER-addon-iamserviceaccount-kube-system-aws-load-balancer-controller.

5

Install the controller

The pod that watches for Ingress objects

terminalhelm
helm upgrade --install aws-load-balancer-controller eks/aws-load-balancer-controller \
  -n kube-system \
  --set clusterName="$CLUSTER" \
  --set region="$REGION" \
  --set vpcId="$VPC" \
  --set serviceAccount.create=false \
  --set serviceAccount.name=aws-load-balancer-controller \
  --wait
FlagWhy it is there
clusterName Required. The controller tags every load balancer with it, and uses it to tell its own resources from someone else's.
region, vpcId It can discover both from instance metadata, but that lookup fails slowly and confusingly. Passing them removes a startup dependency.
serviceAccount.create=false The one that matters. Step 4 already made the service account, with its annotation. Let Helm make a second one and you get a controller with no AWS identity.
--wait Blocks until the pods are actually ready, so a failure surfaces here rather than in step 6.
Check 
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=aws-load-balancer-controller
kubectl get ingressclass

Two pods 1/1 Running, and an IngressClass named alb. Your Ingress refers to that class by name in step 6 — if it is missing, nothing will ever pick the Ingress up.

See IRSA actually working

terminalthe payoff
kubectl get pod -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=aws-load-balancer-controller \
  -o jsonpath='{range .items[0].spec.containers[0].env[*]}{.name}={.value}{"\n"}{end}'

You will see AWS_ROLE_ARN and AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE. Nothing in the Helm chart sets those. A webhook injected them into the pod because of the annotation you checked in step 4 — that is the whole mechanism, visible in one command.

Two things that look broken and are not

kubectl exec … -- env fails with executable file not found. The controller image is distroless — no shell, no env binary. Read the pod spec instead, as above.

The startup log says Disabling ALBGatewayAPI: missing required CRDs. Expected. That is the optional Gateway API feature standing down; Ingress support is unaffected.

6

Create the Ingress

One per application — the only step you repeat

Everything so far was plumbing. This is the object that actually asks for a load balancer. Replace my-app with your Service name and 80 with its port.

ingress.yamlkubernetes
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: my-app
  annotations:
    # internet-facing = a public ALB. Use internal-facing for a private one,
    # which is what the internal-elb subnet tag is for.
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing

    # ip, not instance: pods hold real VPC addresses, so the ALB reaches a
    # pod directly instead of hopping through a NodePort on the host.
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip

    # The path the ALB polls to decide a pod is healthy. Point it at a
    # cheap endpoint, not at your homepage.
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-path: /healthz
spec:
  ingressClassName: alb
  rules:
    - http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: my-app
                port:
                  number: 80
terminalapply
kubectl apply -f ingress.yaml -n "$NAMESPACE"
Trap

Every Service named in the rules must already exist. The controller resolves all of them when it builds its plan, and one missing Service fails the whole thing — you get no load balancer at all, not a partial one. If you are adding a second service later, deploy it first, then add its path.

7

Wait for the address

Two waits, not one

terminalwatch
kubectl get ingress -n "$NAMESPACE" -w

The ADDRESS column is empty at first, then fills with a long …elb.amazonaws.com hostname. That takes 2–3 minutes.

Then wait again. The address appears before the load balancer serves anything — DNS has to propagate and the targets have to pass a first health check. Give it another 1–2 minutes.

terminalconfirm
export ADDR=$(kubectl get ingress my-app -n "$NAMESPACE" \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].hostname}')

echo "http://$ADDR"

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "http://$ADDR/"
Done when

curl prints 200 and the URL opens in a browser. If it prints 000, the DNS name has not propagated yet — wait a minute and try again. If it prints 503, the ALB exists but no target is healthy: check your health check path.

While it is coming up, the controller's log is the only place that explains a failure. The Ingress object itself stays silent:

terminalthe real error is here
kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/aws-load-balancer-controller -f --tail=20
?

When it does not work

Symptom to cause, in order of likelihood

What you seeWhat it actually is
ADDRESS stays empty forever Subnet tags. Redo step 2 — you need two elb: 1 subnets in two different AZs.
failed calling webhook "vingress.elbv2.k8s.aws" … context deadline exceeded The EKS control plane cannot reach the controller's webhook on port 9443. Allow it on the cluster security group.
Controller logs show AccessDenied or NoCredentialProviders IRSA. The service account annotation is missing, or the trust policy names the wrong namespace or service account. Redo the step 4 check.
Controller logs show couldn't auto-discover subnets Step 2 again — but check the cluster tag too. A kubernetes.io/cluster/<name> tag naming a different cluster excludes the subnet.
ALB exists, returns 503 No healthy targets. The health check path returns something other than 200, or your pods are not ready. Check the target group in the EC2 console.
Ingress created but no ALB, no errors A Service named in the rules does not exist, or ingressClassName: alb is missing or misspelled.
Everything worked yesterday, nothing today Your shell variables are gone. Re-run step 0.

The port 9443 fix, since it is the least guessable one:

terminalwebhook fix
export CLUSTER_SG=$(aws eks describe-cluster --name "$CLUSTER" --region "$REGION" \
  --query "cluster.resourcesVpcConfig.clusterSecurityGroupId" --output text)

aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --region "$REGION" \
  --group-id "$CLUSTER_SG" --protocol tcp --port 9443 --source-group "$CLUSTER_SG"
↺

Tearing it down

Order matters here too

Delete the Ingress first

The load balancer is owned by the controller, not by AWS-side automation. Remove the controller while an Ingress still exists and the ALB is orphaned: nothing left in the cluster knows about it, and it keeps billing until somebody finds it in the EC2 console.

terminalin this order
# 1. This is what actually deletes the load balancer
kubectl delete ingress my-app -n "$NAMESPACE"

# 2. Wait until it is gone from AWS before continuing
aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers --region "$REGION" \
  --query "LoadBalancers[].LoadBalancerName" --output text

# 3. Now the controller
helm uninstall aws-load-balancer-controller -n kube-system

# 4. And the CloudFormation stack behind the service account
eksctl delete iamserviceaccount --cluster "$CLUSTER" --region "$REGION" \
  --namespace kube-system --name aws-load-balancer-controller

The IAM policy from step 3 is account-wide and shared. Leave it — it costs nothing and the next cluster will want it.

End of runbook · steps 1–5 once per cluster · step 6 once per app
